slides.page_title: Two Ways Keys Die: Expiry vs Eviction

items: Expiry works fine with `maxmemory` unset.
Eviction can take keys that have no TTL.
Which keys depends on `maxmemory-policy`.
No `maxmemory` + no TTLs = unbounded store, OOM.

blocks.title: Redis is not a cache by default
blocks.text: It is an in-memory store. Cache behaviour is something you configure, not something you get.

items: No TTL = persistent. TTL set = volatile.
Past deadline = invisible to clients, still in RAM.
Memory returns to allocator only on physical delete.
So a TTL alone never gives an instant memory drop.

blocks.title: Logically expired
blocks.text: The central idea of this handbook: after the deadline a key is unreadable but may occupy memory for a while.

items: `DBSIZE` counts logically-expired-but-present keys.
`INFO keyspace` does too — counts exceed what reads see.
Never treat either as authoritative key count.

blocks.title: Carry this through
items: TTL = a promise about visibility.
TTL is not a promise about memory.
TTLs express correctness. Eviction expresses survival.

lines: # never sum these two in a dashboard

items: Commands are single-threaded; nothing preempts a running one.
Eviction compares against `used_memory`, not RSS.
Never assume a key vanished at the exact millisecond.
Across a cluster, deadlines land node by node.
`EXPIRE` returns 1 if set, 0 if key missing.
`PEXPIREAT` is the primitive; all others reduce to it.
Storage is always a millisecond Unix timestamp.

blocks.title: Classic bug
blocks.text: Confusing `-1` (persistent) with `-2` (missing). One means immortal, the other means gone.

items: `PTTL` for millisecond precision on the remainder.
`EXPIRETIME`/`PEXPIRETIME` (7.0+) give the deadline itself.
`PERSIST key` strips the TTL, key becomes persistent.
`PERSIST` returns 1 only if a TTL was really removed.

lines: SET tok:9 abc EX 60      # one round trip
SET tok:9 abc PXAT 1789...  # absolute ms
SET tok:9 xyz KEEPTTL    # keeps old deadline
SET tok:9 xyz            # CLEARS the TTL

items: `EX` / `PX` / `EXAT` / `PXAT` all valid on `SET`.
Atomic form leaves no window where the key is immortal.
`GETEX k EX 60` reads and refreshes in one command.
`GETEX k PERSIST` reads and strips the TTL.

slides.page_title: TTL Condition Flags & What Clears a TTL

items: A persistent key counts as infinite TTL here.
So `GT` never sets a TTL on a persistent key.
And `LT` always does — it is always shorter than infinity.

blocks.q: Extend a session, never accidentally shorten it?
a_bullets: Use `GT` so a stale worker cannot cut the window.
Plain `EXPIRE` would overwrite a longer deadline.
Negative seconds or a past `EXPIREAT` delete now — and report success.

blocks.title: Legacy sugar
items: `SETEX key sec val` = `SET key val EX sec`.
Errors outright if seconds <= 0.
Prefer `SET ... EX` in new code.
Full value replacement drops the deadline.
In-place mutation never touches it.
`SETRANGE` through the SET path clears it too.

blocks.title: The counter trap
blocks.text: `INCR` then `EXPIRE` on every request keeps resetting the window — a rate limiter that never resets.

items: `RENAME src dst` carries the source TTL to `dst`.
It destroys whatever TTL `dst` had.
`COPY src dst` does not copy the TTL — `dst` is persistent.
`DEL` then recreate = TTL gone, key starts persistent.

blocks.title: Plain SET after EXPIRE
blocks.text: The overwrite ==clears== the deadline and the key becomes **immortal**. Use `KEEPTTL` or set both atomically.

items: `SET` on a volatile key without `KEEPTTL`.
`EXPIRE` on every `INCR` — window slides forever.
Reading `-1` as 'missing' and recreating the key.
Expecting `COPY` to carry the deadline across.

slides.page_title: TTL Semantics: What Resets, What Survives

items: You cannot expire one hash field, list element or set member.
Redis 7.4 `HEXPIRE` adds per-field hash TTLs — hashes only.
A giant hash or ZSET is otherwise all-or-nothing.
Model per-item expiry as separate keys, or sweep manually.

lines: DEL job:3 job:5             # then drop them

blocks.title: ZSET sweeper pattern
items: Score = absolute deadline.
Poll `ZRANGEBYSCORE idx -inf now`.
Gives per-member expiry with explicit control.
Reading a key never extends its TTL. Redis has no sliding mode.
Want touch-to-refresh? Call `GETEX key EX n` explicitly.
`FLUSHDB`/`FLUSHALL` remove everything, TTLs included.
`SWAPDB` moves the keyspace; deadlines survive, they are absolute.
TTLs live in a separate `expires` dict keyed by the same object.
A persistent key therefore costs zero TTL memory.
A volatile key costs ~one extra dict entry, tens of bytes.
Millions of short TTLs is a real memory line item.

blocks.title: Clock hazard
blocks.text: Deadlines are absolute. A server clock jump forward mass-expires keys; a jump backward strands them.

items: Every keyspace lookup calls `expireIfNeeded()` first.
Past the deadline, the key is deleted right there.
The command behaves as if the key never existed.
Cost: O(1) amortised per access, zero background work.

blocks.title: Why lazy is primary
blocks.text: It piggybacks on work you already pay for. No sweep, no scan, no extra CPU when idle.

blocks.title: The flaw
blocks.text: A key never touched again is never lazily expired. Write-once, never-read keys leak forever without active expiry.

items: The primary sends an explicit `DEL` to replicas and the AOF.
Removal is a real replicated write, not an implicit rule.
Since Redis 6 it is `UNLINK` when `lazyfree-lazy-expire yes`.
Otherwise it stays a plain synchronous `DEL`.
A replica's `DBSIZE` can legitimately exceed its primary's.
That is by design — not a bug, not drift.
Before Redis 3.2 replicas served stale expired reads.
Modern replicas filter them at read time instead.

blocks.title: Writable replicas
items: Keep a local `expires` dict for locally-written keys.
Rarely used, easily misunderstood corner.
Avoid unless you know exactly why.

lines: local b = redis.call('GET', KEYS[1])  -- same result

items: A key cannot expire mid-script; scripts stay deterministic.
Functions get the same guarantee as Lua `EVAL`.
`MULTI`/`EXEC` also evaluates expiry once, not between commands.

slides.page_title: Active Expiry: The Sampling Loop & the 25% Rule

items: Freeing a 10M-element set synchronously stalls the loop hundreds of ms.
`lazyfree-lazy-expire yes` moves the free to a background thread.
Turn it on whenever values are large collections.

blocks.q: Is this expiry or memory pressure?
a_bullets: `expired_keys` rising, `evicted_keys` flat = expiry doing its job.
Both rising = TTLs are not keeping up with the ceiling.
`OBJECT FREQ` and `DEBUG SLEEP` help only after you know which.

items: `activeExpireCycle()` runs inside `serverCron`, `hz 10` by default.
So roughly ten passes per second, per database.
Samples `ACTIVE_EXPIRE_CYCLE_KEYS_PER_LOOP` = 20 random keys.
It samples the `expires` dict, never the main dict.

blocks.title: Cost scales with volatile keys
blocks.text: A 100M-key DB with 1000 TTLs samples from those 1000. Persistent keys cost the cycle nothing.

items: Delete the expired ones from the sample, then measure the ratio.
Above 25% expired: immediately repeat the loop on that DB.
Below 25%: move on to the next database.
It is a probabilistic guarantee, not a deadline guarantee.

blocks.title: What 25% buys
blocks.text: At steady state, expected expired-but-present keys stay under ~25% of the volatile keyspace.

lines: # more keys per loop, more CPU

slides.page_title: Fast vs Slow Cycles & Expiry Effort

items: Fast cycle shaves latency spikes between cron ticks.
Slow cycle capped by `ACTIVE_EXPIRE_CYCLE_SLOW_TIME_PERC`.
So expiry can never starve command processing.
Redis 6+ adds an effort dial and an early bail-out check.
Higher effort samples more keys and tolerates fewer stale ones.
Costs extra CPU in both fast and slow cycles.
Raise it only when stale keys visibly bloat `used_memory`.

blocks.title: Is the cycle keeping up?
blocks.text: `INFO stats` shows ==`expired_stale_perc`== (estimated stale share) and `expired_time_cap_reached_count` — a rising cap count means the cycle keeps hitting its CPU limit.

slides.page_title: Tuning hz, TTL Jitter & the maxmemory Ceiling

lines: CONFIG SET hz 100        # 10x more cron ticks
CONFIG SET dynamic-hz yes  # scale with client count
# smoother memory, steady background CPU cost

items: Random sampling means no priority by remaining TTL.
A 1-second key is not guaranteed reclaimed before a 10-minute one.
Redis 6 also checks for keys about to expire, to exit early.

blocks.title: Pathological case
blocks.text: Millions of keys sharing one absolute deadline: all fire at once, the cycle burns its 25% for seconds, latency spikes.

lines: r.expire(key, ttl)  # jitter, same trick as stampedes

items: Uniform TTLs → synchronised expiry and a **CPU** spike.
Same moment → a replication-traffic burst to every replica.
Same moment → a cache stampede hitting your backend.

blocks.title: The real contract
items: Active expiry deletes on the primary only.
Every deletion replicates — mass expiry = traffic burst.
Lazy + active: invisible at the deadline, reclaimed soon after.
No upper bound on 'soon' is guaranteed.

lines: CONFIG SET maxmemory 2gb # runtime, evicts now

items: `maxmemory 0` is the setting most incidents trace back to.
Units like `2gb` are accepted in config and `CONFIG SET`.
Lowering it at runtime can trigger immediate mass eviction.
Compared against `used_memory`, as jemalloc reports it.

slides.page_title: The Eviction Loop, OOM Errors & Headroom

blocks.title: Not RSS
blocks.text: The comparison subtracts replication buffers and AOF buffer overhead. Process RSS is a different number.

items: `performEvictions()` runs before each command that may grow memory.
Victim chosen by policy, removal propagated as `DEL`/`UNLINK`.
Loop continues until under the limit or nothing is freeable.
Happens under `noeviction`, or when every key is protected.
Reads and `DEL` still succeed — you can dig out.
`lazyfree-lazy-eviction yes` frees big victims off-thread.
Forking for `BGSAVE` can ==double RSS== via copy-on-write.
So set `maxmemory` to ~50-60% of box RAM if you fork.
`maxmemory-clients` (7.0) caps client buffers separately.
High `mem_fragmentation_ratio`? Use `activedefrag`, not eviction.

caption.text: Your Redis key did not disappear at its deadline — it just became invisible. This handbook walks the whole death pipeline: the TTL command surface and the flags that quietly clear it, the lazy and active expiry cycles that actually reclaim memory, and how maxmemory turns 'soon' into a hard budget under approximated LRU and LFU. Ten pages of internals, sampling math, and the six mistakes that cause silent data loss or an OOM at 3am.
